title: Ötzi’s Living Legacy: Cold-Loving Yeasts Still Thrive on the Iceman
summary:
Ötzi the Iceman, the famous 5,300-year-old mummy discovered in the Alps in 1991, isn’t as lifeless as he seems. A team led by Eurac Research’s Institute for Mummy Studies has found that his body still harbors living microorganisms—specifically, cold-adapted yeasts that probably came from the glacier where he lay frozen. Published in the journal *Microbiome*, the study used DNA analysis on samples from Ötzi’s skin, internal meltwater, stomach contents, and even soil from the discovery site.

The researchers were initially mapping Ötzi’s ancient gut microbiome—the community of bacteria that lived inside him when he was alive. That microbiome, first described in 2019, resembles those of early human populations and is rarely seen in modern industrialized societies. But the surprise came from the yeasts. Genetic testing showed they are closely related to strains found in extremely cold environments like Antarctica, strongly suggesting they originated in the glacier and have remained with the mummy ever since.

What’s remarkable is that these yeasts aren’t just ancient DNA fragments; they appear to be alive. The team detected both degraded (old) and well-preserved (modern) genetic material, indicating the organisms are surviving—perhaps in a dormant state—under the mummy’s current storage conditions of -6°C and high humidity. “We see continuity here,” explains Frank Maixner, director of the institute. “These yeasts have accompanied Ötzi on his long journey through the millennia.” He adds that the mummy is “not a static relic, but a dynamic biological system.”

Interestingly, three of the four yeast species can break down phenol, a chemical used in past conservation efforts to remove fungal growth. The yeasts may have actually fed on this substance, turning a preservative into a food source. This accidental cultivation highlights how human intervention can shape a mummy’s microbiome.

Beyond the wow factor, these hardy yeasts could have practical uses. Their ability to thrive in cold and metabolize unusual compounds makes them candidates for industrial processes, such as bioremediation or pharmaceutical production. Ötzi, it seems, still has secrets to share—and some of them are alive and kicking.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows that even ancient remains can act as living laboratories, offering microorganisms that might lead to new antibiotics or industrial enzymes, and it reminds us that life finds a way to survive in the most extreme places—even on a mummy.

background_read: Ötzi was found by hikers in the Ötztal Alps on the border of Italy and Austria, and his remarkably preserved body has been studied at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano, Italy.

Early studies revealed his last meal, his health, and how he died from an arrow wound. In 2019, scientists at Eurac Research's Institute for Mummy Studies (the leading center for studying the Iceman) decoded his gut microbiome, finding bacteria typical of ancient human populations that rarely appear in modern gut samples.

Now, they have discovered that Ötzi's body still hosts living yeasts that likely came from the glacier where he lay frozen for millennia. These yeasts are close relatives of strains found in Antarctica, showing how microorganisms can survive extreme cold.

The discovery adds a new layer to our understanding of mummies as not static remains but active biological environments. Frank Maixner, director of the institute, noted that the yeasts may have fed on phenol used in past conservation efforts, turning a preservative into food.

perspectives.description: These hardy yeasts could be harnessed for cleaning up polluted environments or making medicines, offering a practical benefit from studying ancient remains while also teaching us about extremophile survival.

The accidental feeding of yeasts on conservation chemicals shows that human attempts to preserve history can alter the very biology we aim to study, potentially contaminating valuable samples and muddying scientific conclusions.

The fact that Ötzi's microbiome has changed from his living state to modern contaminants illustrates how archaeological specimens are not frozen in time but evolve even in museums, complicating the search for truly ancient microbes.

Future research might deliberately isolate and culture these yeasts for biotech applications, and similar techniques could be used on other mummies worldwide to uncover living extremophiles with industrial potential.
